summary: This Informational report covers the IAB's three-day online NEMOPS workshop held in December 2024. It builds on the 2002 workshop documented in RFC 3535, which listed operator requirements for network management, and looks at what has changed since.

eli5.summary: Experts met online for three days to talk about how to run big networks and wrote down what they discussed.

questions: next era of network management operations
how has network management changed since 2002
what are operator requirements for network management
subtitle: Following up on network management operator requirements two decades later.

tldr.problem: Network management has evolved significantly since 2002 (RFC 3535). Today's operators face new challenges with complex protocols, fragmented tooling, and the need to balance standardization with rapid innovation.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB convened the NEMOPS workshop in December 2024 to review what worked since RFC 3535, identify operational barriers preventing technology adoption, and develop new recommendations for network management.
tldr.outcome: The workshop found that while YANG and NETCONF succeeded in device configuration, gaps remain in monitoring, service-level management, tooling, and agile development processes. Key recommendations focus on reducing complexity, improving tooling, and enabling faster iteration.

facts.value: Over 60 network operators, vendors, and protocol engineers

today: RFC 9968 is an Informational document published in May 2026 that guides the IETF's ongoing work on network management. It remains current guidance for operators, standards bodies, and vendors seeking to understand the challenges and opportunities in modern network management.

sections.title: Introduction: The NEMOPS Workshop
sections.content:
The IAB held the Next Era of Network Management Operations (NEMOPS) workshop in December 2024 to assess the state of network management. This workshop directly follows the 2002 workshop documented in RFC 3535, which identified 14 operator requirements and sparked the development of NETCONF, YANG, RESTCONF, and other management technologies.

The 2024 workshop asked three central questions: What has changed since 2002? What barriers prevent these technologies from being widely used? What new recommendations should guide the IETF? The workshop brought together network operators, vendors, protocol engineers, and the IAB to share diverse perspectives on network management challenges and opportunities.
sections.eli5: The workshop was a follow-up meeting 20 years later to check if old advice was still good and to figure out what new advice was needed.

sections.title: Background: What Worked and What Didn't Since 2002
sections.content:
RFC 3535 recommended YANG and NETCONF as solutions for network management. These technologies have succeeded in device-level configuration: many network devices now support YANG models and NETCONF protocols, and streaming telemetry has even surpassed the original scope of RFC 3535 in some deployments.

However, significant gaps remain. Participants noted that YANG models work well for provisioning but fall short for operational monitoring and validation. Vendor YANG models often diverge from IETF and OpenConfig standards, creating complexity. Many network operators still rely on CLI (command-line interfaces), Ansible, and SNMP rather than modern management protocols. The lack of open-source network management tools and the steep learning curve for these technologies have limited adoption, especially in smaller networks.
sections.eli5: Some things worked great: devices can now be configured with a standard way called YANG. But other things are stuck: everyone still uses old ways because the new tools are hard to use and don't work the same way everywhere.

sections.title: Today's Challenges for Network Operators
sections.content:
The workshop identified several recurring problems. First, fragmentation is pervasive: operators must juggle SNMP, NETCONF, RESTCONF, gNMI, streaming telemetry, and other protocols. There is no agreed-upon solution stack for common use cases. Second, tooling is inadequate: there is a lack of user-friendly, open-source network management tools, especially for smaller operators. Third, service-level modeling is immature: while device-level models exist, the industry struggles with service-level abstractions that operators actually care about.

Fourth, vendor diversity creates complexity: operators must support multiple data models (IETF, OpenConfig, and vendor-specific models) simultaneously, with inconsistent mappings and limited interoperability testing. Fifth, rapid innovation is constrained by the slow RFC publication process. Vendors and operators want to iterate faster, but IETF standards development takes time, preventing YANG models from keeping pace with software updates and new features.
sections.eli5: Operators complained that there are too many different tools to learn, the tools don't work well together, and it takes too long to make new standards when things change fast.

sections.title: Key Recommendations for the IETF
sections.content:
The workshop consensus produced four categories of recommendations. Ecosystem recommendations include continuing to focus on model-driven management, introducing 'running code' as a verification requirement, having vendors support a recommended solution stack, and improving documentation and training. Protocol recommendations emphasize that NETCONF and YANG should expand beyond device configuration to cover monitoring, and that push-based solutions (like YANG-Push) should gain wider adoption.

Modeling recommendations focus on reducing complexity, achieving multi-vendor compatibility, supporting service-level modeling, enabling configuration validation, and using off-box adapters to map standard models to vendor-specific implementations. Standardization recommendations call for faster, more agile development procedures; exploring models outside RFC formats (such as on GitHub); reducing protocol and model complexity to essential features; and grounding enhancements in real-world use cases and vendor commitment.
sections.eli5: The experts recommended that the organizations making standards should: focus on making tools easier to use, support running actual code to test new ideas, work with vendors on a common approach, speed up how fast standards are made, and keep things simpler.

sections.title: Emerging Approaches and Next Steps
sections.content:
Several forward-looking ideas emerged from the workshop. One proposal uses knowledge graphs based on the Semantic Web Stack to integrate data models across silos and protocols, making semantics machine-readable. Another prioritizes RESTCONF+JSON and YANG-Push Lite as a single preferred protocol, along with Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) adoption and off-box data model adapters.

There was also recognition that IETF standards development itself needs experimentation. Instead of top-down mandates, the workshop suggested allowing working groups and areas to test new, faster development processes, manage YANG modules as code or APIs (not embedded in RFCs), and maintain standard model mapping in common repositories so the community can assess coverage and alignment. These changes aim to reduce unnecessary complexity, accelerate feature deployment, and foster better collaboration between vendors and operators.
sections.eli5: The workshop suggested trying new ideas like using knowledge graphs to connect different models, picking one main protocol instead of many, managing standards code like software projects, and letting different groups experiment with faster ways of making standards.
